questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies the mechanism of acetazolamide. Which best describes its molecular target?
explanations: Incorrect. ENaC is the K+-sparing diuretic target.
Incorrect. NKCC2 is the loop diuretic target.

Correct. Acetazolamide and other CA inhibitors block carbonic anhydrase isoforms (principally CA II intracellular and CA IV at the brush border). In the proximal tubule this impairs HCO3− reabsorption (the dehydration of luminal H2CO3 to CO2 + H2O is blocked) and reduces H+ secretion via NHE3. Result: bicarbonaturia, mild diuresis, alkaline urine, and mild metabolic acidosis. Other CA inhibitors: methazolamide (oral), dorzolamide and brinzolamide (topical for glaucoma).
Incorrect. Aldosterone receptor is the spironolactone target.
Incorrect. AQP2 is the V2 antagonist target.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with acute angle-closure glaucoma has IOP 50 mm Hg. The ophthalmologist gives IV acetazolamide. Which best explains the mechanism of IOP reduction?
explanations: Incorrect. Mannitol is a separate osmotic agent.

Correct. Carbonic anhydrase is highly expressed in the ciliary body, where it generates HCO3− needed for aqueous humor formation. CA inhibition reduces aqueous humor production by ~30%, lowering IOP. Used for: acute angle-closure glaucoma (IV/oral as adjunct to topical agents and definitive iridotomy), chronic open-angle glaucoma (topical dorzolamide, brinzolamide). Other glaucoma drug classes: β-blockers (timolol — also reduce production), prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost — increase outflow), α2-agonists (brimonidine), miotics (pilocarpine).
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not principally affect outflow.
Incorrect. Optic nerve is downstream of pressure reduction.
Incorrect. Lens dehydration is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old climber takes acetazolamide before ascending to high altitude. Which best explains the mechanism of altitude prophylaxis?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not directly dilate cerebral vessels.

Correct. At altitude, low PO2 → hypoxic hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis. Renal compensation (HCO3− loss) takes days; in the meantime, alkalosis blunts the hypoxic ventilatory drive, slowing acclimatization. Acetazolamide induces a metabolic acidosis (bicarbonaturia) — this offsets the alkalosis, restores hypoxic drive, and accelerates ventilation. Reduces incidence and severity of acute mountain sickness. Dose 125–250 mg BID; start 24–48 h before ascent and continue for 2 days at altitude.
Incorrect. No erythropoietic effect.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not increase Hb-O2 affinity.
Incorrect. O2 demand is not principally reduced.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) has headache, papilledema, and elevated CSF pressure on lumbar puncture. Which medication is first-line?
explanations: Correct. Acetazolamide is first-line for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). Mechanism: CA inhibition reduces CSF production at the choroid plexus (which expresses CA), lowering intracranial pressure. Dose typically 1–4 g/day. Adjuncts: weight loss (the most effective long-term), possibly topiramate (also CA inhibitor + weight loss effects); refractory cases may need surgical CSF diversion (LP shunt, VP shunt) or optic nerve sheath fenestration. Vision loss is the principal complication of IIH.
Incorrect. Furosemide is sometimes added as adjunct but not first-line.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is not first-line.
Incorrect. Mannitol is for acute ICP elevation in TBI, not chronic IIH.
Incorrect. Dorzolamide is topical (for glaucoma), not effective systemically.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic acetazolamide therapy for glaucoma has pH 7.32, HCO3− 18, Cl− 110, anion gap 10. Which best characterizes the acid-base disorder?
explanations: Incorrect. No hypoperfusion described; AG is normal.

Correct. Chronic acetazolamide therapy produces a mild non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis through bicarbonaturia (mimicking proximal RTA). The renal threshold for HCO3− reabsorption is reduced. Effect is dose-related and self-limited (the acidosis itself reduces drug efficacy, allowing equilibrium). Acidosis is generally mild and well-tolerated; severe cases may need dose reduction or alternation. Same mechanism in topiramate (a weak CA inhibitor used for migraine, seizures).
Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features urine pH inappropriately high (>5.5).
Incorrect. DKA has hyperglycemia and ketones.
Incorrect. No diarrhea history.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on chronic acetazolamide develops Ca-phosphate kidney stones. Which mechanism best explains the increased stone risk?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not chemically chelate Ca2+.

Correct. Acetazolamide alkalinizes urine (urine pH often >7.0) AND can increase urinary calcium excretion (mild diuretic effect, contraction-effect mild) AND reduces urinary citrate (citrate is a stone inhibitor; its excretion falls in metabolic acidosis). Combined effects favor calcium phosphate stone formation. Topiramate (also CA inhibitor) carries similar risk. Counsel patients on hydration; avoid in patients with prior calcium phosphate stones.
Incorrect. Direct precipitation is not the mechanism.
Incorrect. Hyperoxaluria is not the principal mechanism.
Incorrect. Uricosuria is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on chronic acetazolamide has K+ 3.2. Which mechanism best explains the hypokalemia?
choices: Distal Na+ delivery and aldosterone effect
explanations: Incorrect. Mechanism is indirect (distal flow + aldosterone).

Correct. Acetazolamide blocks proximal HCO3− and Na+ reabsorption, increasing distal Na+ delivery. The collecting duct then reabsorbs Na+ via ENaC and secretes K+ via ROMK; aldosterone activated by mild volume contraction enhances this. Net effect: renal K+ wasting and mild hypokalemia. Same mechanism by which other diuretics produce hypokalemia. Mitigation: K+ supplementation, K+-sparing diuretic combination.
Incorrect. Direct ROMK activation is not the mechanism.
Incorrect. No GI losses described.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not principally cause cellular K+ shift.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman on acetazolamide reports tingling around the lips and fingers. Which best explains this paresthesia?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not principally lower Ca2+.

Correct. Paresthesias are a recognized acetazolamide side effect, related to CA inhibition in red cells and tissue capillaries → impaired CO2 transport → mild tissue CO2 buildup with paresthesias particularly perioral and acral. Usually mild and self-limited. Other CA-related effects: dysgeusia (carbonated drinks taste 'flat'), fatigue.
Incorrect. Sulfa allergy presents as rash, urticaria, or anaphylaxis — not paresthesias alone.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not principally cause hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. The paresthesia has a pharmacologic explanation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with severe sulfa allergy is being considered for acetazolamide for altitude sickness. Which best characterizes acetazolamide and sulfa allergy?
choices: Acetazolamide is safe in any sulfa allergy
Acetazolamide is sulfonamide-derived; caution in severe allergy
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide IS a sulfonamide.

Correct. Acetazolamide is a sulfonamide-derived drug. In patients with documented severe sulfa allergy (anaphylaxis to antibacterial sulfonamides), caution is warranted — though cross-reactivity between antibacterial sulfonamides and non-antibacterial sulfonamides (acetazolamide, thiazides, loops) is uncommon, severe reactions have been reported. For mild or self-reported sulfa allergy, acetazolamide is usually tolerated. Document the type and severity of prior reaction. Alternative for altitude sickness: dexamethasone.
Incorrect. Allergy is relevant for severe cases.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not neutralize allergy.
Incorrect. The interaction concern is anaphylaxis, not efficacy reduction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with severe HF and refractory metabolic alkalosis from chronic loop diuretic has pH 7.55, HCO3− 38. Acetazolamide is added. Which best characterizes its role?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not first-line for all alkalosis.

Correct. In refractory metabolic alkalosis where saline + KCl repletion is contraindicated (e.g., HF with volume overload), acetazolamide can correct alkalosis through bicarbonaturia. Useful when loop diuretic-induced alkalosis cannot be addressed by adding more volume. Watch for hypokalemia (acetazolamide adds to the K+ wasting). Adjust loop diuretic dose simultaneously. Severe refractory alkalosis may need IV HCl in selected cases.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is additive but not principally for synergy with loop in HF.
Incorrect. Does not replace loop.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not for hypocapnia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with chronic open-angle glaucoma is using topical dorzolamide. Which best characterizes topical CA inhibitors?
choices: Topical CA inhibitors with minimal systemic effects
Same systemic side effects as oral acetazolamide
explanations: Correct. Topical CA inhibitors (dorzolamide, brinzolamide) reduce aqueous humor production locally with minimal systemic absorption — fewer systemic effects (no metabolic acidosis, no significant K+ wasting, no paresthesias) compared with oral acetazolamide. Used for chronic open-angle glaucoma. Local side effects: ocular irritation, bitter taste, allergic conjunctivitis. Caution still warranted in severe sulfa allergy.
Incorrect. Topical use minimizes systemic effects.
Incorrect. Topical agents are not first-line for acute angle-closure (oral/IV needed for the acute pressure).
Incorrect. Altitude requires systemic absorption.
Incorrect. Topical CA inhibitors are effective in chronic glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers acetazolamide effects on K+ secretion. Which best characterizes the drug's K+ effects compared with loop and thiazide diuretics?
choices: K+ wasting via distal Na+ delivery
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide is K+-wasting, not K+-sparing.

Correct. All diuretics that increase distal Na+ delivery (acetazolamide, loop, thiazide) produce K+ wasting via aldosterone-driven principal cell K+ secretion. Acetazolamide's K+ effect is generally milder than loop or thiazide because its diuretic effect is weaker. Combined with K+-sparing diuretic (amiloride) or K+ supplementation in chronic use.
Incorrect. Effect is real.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not K+-retaining.
Incorrect. Mechanism is indirect.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis has recurrent attacks of acute weakness. Acetazolamide is started prophylactically. Which best explains its role?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide is principally prophylactic.

Correct. In familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis (autosomal dominant mutations in CACNA1S or SCN4A), acetazolamide reduces attack frequency. The mild metabolic acidosis from CA inhibition stabilizes muscle membrane and prevents the K+ shifts that precipitate attacks. Avoidance of triggers (high carbohydrate meals, rest after exercise, cold) is also important. K+-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone) are alternatives.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not directly replace K+.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is therapeutic.
Incorrect. Does not change the genetics.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man on chronic topiramate for migraine has paresthesias, mild metabolic acidosis, and a kidney stone. Which best characterizes topiramate's effect on the kidney?
choices: Topiramate is unrelated to renal function
explanations: Incorrect. Topiramate has renal effects.

Correct. Topiramate (anticonvulsant, migraine prophylaxis) has weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor activity, producing similar effects to acetazolamide: mild metabolic acidosis, alkaline urine, hypokalemia, and Ca-phosphate kidney stones. Recognized as a stone risk in patients on long-term therapy. Other neurologic uses: weight loss (often a desired side effect), seizures.
Incorrect. Topiramate is not a loop diuretic.
Incorrect. Topiramate does not raise Ca2+.
Incorrect. Type 4 RTA is hyperkalemic; topiramate causes hypokalemic acidosis (mimicking proximal RTA).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher considers acetazolamide effects on ammonia excretion. Which best characterizes this?
choices: NH4+ excretion follows urine pH only
explanations: Incorrect. NH4+ excretion is reduced.

Correct. Acetazolamide alkalinizes urine, reducing the diffusion trap that normally captures NH4+ in tubular fluid (NH3 + H+ → NH4+ in acidic urine). Reduced NH4+ excretion can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis (rising plasma ammonia). For this reason, acetazolamide is contraindicated or used cautiously in advanced liver disease. Alternative: amiloride, mannitol, or other agents.
Incorrect. Effect is real.
Incorrect. Effect is not solely pH-mediated.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not degrade NH4+.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites is being started on a diuretic. Which CA inhibitor concern applies?
choices: Avoid acetazolamide due to encephalopathy risk
Acetazolamide is unrelated to liver function
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone + furosemide (100:40) is first-line for cirrhotic ascites.

Correct. Acetazolamide alkalinizes urine and reduces NH4+ excretion, raising plasma ammonia. In cirrhosis with already-impaired hepatic ammonia clearance, this can precipitate or worsen HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY. Use is generally avoided in advanced liver disease. Cirrhotic ascites is best treated with spironolactone + furosemide in 100:40 ratio.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is preferred.
Incorrect. Not liver-protective.
Incorrect. Liver disease is a relative contraindication.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient is given acetazolamide for urinary alkalinization in salicylate poisoning. Which best characterizes this practice?
choices: Standard first-line therapy for salicylate poisoning
explanations: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate is preferred.

Correct. For salicylate poisoning, the goal is urinary alkalinization to ion-trap salicylate (a weak acid) in alkaline urine, increasing renal clearance. Sodium bicarbonate (typically 1–2 mEq/kg bolus then infusion) is preferred — it directly alkalinizes urine AND raises plasma pH (reducing salicylate's CNS distribution). Acetazolamide alkalinizes urine but DROPS plasma pH (metabolic acidosis), which would WORSEN salicylate CNS toxicity. Hemodialysis is reserved for severe cases.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not strictly contraindicated but is not preferred.
Incorrect. Mechanism is alkalinization, not direct salicylate effect.
Incorrect. They are not interchangeable.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher reviews acetazolamide effects on phosphate. Which best characterizes the effect?
explanations: Incorrect. Phosphate falls.

Correct. Acetazolamide reduces NaPi-IIa-mediated phosphate reabsorption in the PCT (CA inhibition reduces Na+ entry, secondarily reducing Na+-dependent phosphate transport). Mild hypophosphatemia and increased urinary phosphate excretion can occur. In chronic use, may contribute to bone effects and stone formation. Generally clinically minor.
Incorrect. Effect is real.
Incorrect. Phosphate is excreted, not consumed.
Incorrect. Opposite direction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient is given IV acetazolamide for severe metabolic alkalosis. Which best characterizes the typical dose and onset?
choices: Same dose as oral with identical kinetics
explanations: Incorrect. 5 g is excessive.

Correct. IV acetazolamide for refractory metabolic alkalosis: typical dose 250–500 mg IV, onset 1–2 hours, peak effect 4–6 hours, duration 6–12 hours. Effect: bicarbonaturia and modest reduction in HCO3− over 24 hours. Watch for hypokalemia, paresthesias. Repeat dosing or scheduled regimen for sustained effect. Oral form has similar effect with slower onset (~1 hour to peak).
Incorrect. Bolus dosing is standard.
Incorrect. Same target effect but kinetics differ slightly.
Incorrect. Standard dose is fixed; weight-based adjustment unusual.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers when acetazolamide is contraindicated. Which best lists relative contraindications?
explanations: Incorrect. Multiple cautions exist.

Correct. Relative contraindications and cautions: SEVERE SULFA ALLERGY (acetazolamide is sulfonamide-derived); SEVERE LIVER DISEASE (risk of hepatic encephalopathy from reduced NH4+ excretion); EXISTING HYPERCHLOREMIC METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (acetazolamide will worsen); EXISTING HYPOKALEMIA (acetazolamide will worsen); SEVERE COPD with chronic respiratory acidosis (acetazolamide adds metabolic acidosis); KIDNEY STONES (especially Ca-phosphate); pregnancy category C. Use lower doses or avoid in advanced renal failure.
Incorrect. More contraindications.
Incorrect. More than just renal failure.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is used IN acute glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receives a diuretic challenge with acetazolamide as part of evaluating renal HCO3− handling. Which best characterizes the expected response?
explanations: Correct. Acetazolamide challenge typically produces a marked increase in urinary HCO3− excretion (from <5% of filtered load to ~30%) and a rise in urine pH from ~5.5 to ~7.5 within hours. This response can be used to test PCT HCO3− handling integrity. Diminished response in proximal RTA / Fanconi syndrome suggests baseline impaired PCT function.
Incorrect. Reverse — bicarbonaturia is expected.
Incorrect. Urine pH rises with HCO3− loss.
Incorrect. Mild diuresis is expected.
Incorrect. Urine becomes alkaline.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher considers acetazolamide effects on the eye in chronic open-angle glaucoma. Which best characterizes long-term oral acetazolamide?
explanations: Incorrect. Topical agents are first-line.

Correct. Long-term oral acetazolamide for glaucoma is RESERVED for refractory cases or as bridge therapy due to systemic side effects (paresthesias, fatigue, K+ wasting, metabolic acidosis, stones). First-line agents for chronic open-angle glaucoma: prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost — increase outflow), β-blockers (timolol — decrease production), α2-agonists (brimonidine), TOPICAL CA inhibitors (dorzolamide, brinzolamide — minimal systemic effect), miotics (pilocarpine; rarely first-line). Surgery / laser for refractory.
Incorrect. Glaucoma is managed, not cured.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide effectively lowers IOP.
Incorrect. Not for cataracts.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher considers acetazolamide's effect in patients with COPD. Which best characterizes the recommendation?
choices: Selectively used; not in respiratory failure
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not COPD therapy.

Correct. Acetazolamide can be used cautiously to correct metabolic alkalosis in COPD patients on chronic loop diuretic (post-hypercapnic, contraction alkalosis). It is NOT indicated to treat active hypercapnic respiratory failure (would add metabolic acidosis to the existing respiratory acidosis, worsening the situation). In selected cases of chronic compensation issues, low-dose acetazolamide can help wean ventilator-dependent patients with mixed disorders.
Incorrect. Selectively used.
Incorrect. Not bronchodilator.
Incorrect. Not a replacement.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews CA inhibitor pharmacology. Which characterizes the bioavailability and excretion of acetazolamide?
choices: Poorly absorbed orally; metabolized by liver
explanations: Incorrect. Well-absorbed.

Correct. Acetazolamide is well-absorbed orally with bioavailability ~100%. Highly protein-bound (~90%). Excreted unchanged in urine (renal clearance). Half-life 6–13 hours. Dose adjustment in renal impairment. Formulations: oral tablets (125, 250 mg), extended-release (500 mg), IV (250 mg/mL). Methazolamide: similar but more lipophilic with longer half-life (~14 hours).
Incorrect. Renal excretion, not metabolism.
Incorrect. Renal not GI elimination.
Incorrect. Excreted unchanged.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher reviews the principal indications for CA inhibitors. Which best lists them?
explanations: Incorrect. Multiple indications.

Correct. CA inhibitor indications: GLAUCOMA (acute angle-closure: oral/IV; chronic open-angle: topical preferred); ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS prevention/treatment; IDIOPATHIC INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION (pseudotumor cerebri); URINARY ALKALINIZATION (rarely first-line; bicarbonate preferred); REFRACTORY METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (especially HF with diuretic-induced); HYPOKALEMIC PERIODIC PARALYSIS prophylaxis; URIC ACID and CYSTINE STONE prevention via alkalinization; weak diuretic adjunct (rarely used as monotherapy). Topiramate has weak CA activity used for migraine and seizures.
Incorrect. Not for HTN principally.
Incorrect. Topiramate has CA activity but the primary CA inhibitor indications are not seizures.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is rarely used as diuretic monotherapy.
